Short run, about 16 minutes. 2 screens used, neither passed, so nothing new went into the catalog.

Method: I took the mean normalized embedding of seven token groups (code, math, Chinese, Russian, Japanese, English prose, facts) and dotted it with each layer's router gate weights. In two places this matched the routing scan without being tuned to it: L14 experts {3,4,25} for code and L12 expert 30 for math. Ablating them did almost nothing, though (code .043, math .021), so experts in the middle layers look redundant for these skills.

Final-layer (L23) expert findings:
- **Expert 21: Russian/Cyrillic output.** Ablating it alone dropped en_to_ru_word .907, every other skill moved .03 or less, and random same-size parts moved about 0. The screen still failed because the ru control's score moved by .498 (limit ±.302). Probably an artifact of the control's tiny base score (.022). A better ru control would likely let this expert pass.

- **Experts {5,29}: Japanese output, not separable.** ja .261, but facts (.122) and two_digit_addition (.102) also dropped, and one random part dropped ja .296. Screen failed. Adding expert 17 raised ja to .54 but also addition to .375.

args.summary:
No new parts passed this run. I used 2 of 7 screens and both failed. Three of the findings below are still worth a follow-up.

**Method.** I dotted the mean normalized embedding of seven token groups (code, math, zh, ru, ja, English prose, facts) with each layer's router gate weights. The predicted experts often matched the routing scan without being tuned to it:
- L14 experts {3,4,25} for code
- L12 expert 30 for math
- L22 expert 8 for zh
- L20 expert 31 for ja
- L23 experts 5 and 29 for ja

But in layers 10–22 these experts barely mattered when ablated (drops of .02–.14). Only the final layer (L23) had expert sets with large causal effects.

**Final-layer (L23) expert findings:**
- **Expert 21: Russian/Cyrillic output.** Ablating it alone dropped en_to_ru_word by .907. Every other skill moved .03 or less, and random same-size parts moved ~0. The screen failed only because the ru control's score moved by .498 (limit ±.302); that control's base score is just .022. With a stronger ru control this expert would likely pass. It should be grown into a set with experts 13 and 30, whose router rows also align with Cyrillic tokens.
- **Experts {1,21}: German + Russian output** (de .675, ru .907). Expert 1 is the German half; the already-passed German set L23 [1,4,11] includes it.
- **Experts {1,12,21}: a shared non-Latin translation-output hub.** Drops: ru .91, de .68, zh .43, ja .30. Expert 12 serves both zh and ja.
- **Experts {5,29}: Japanese output, but the screen failed.** ja dropped .261, but facts (.122) and addition (.102) also leaked, and one random part dropped ja by .296. Adding expert 17 raised the ja drop to .54 but also took addition to .375.
- **Experts {8,25,27,28}: broad Latin-script word output.** Drops: fr .86, de .60, it .24, general_text .25, code .15. Not selective.

**Negative results:**
- Router-predicted mid-layer code sets (L10 {17,19,29,30}, L14 {3,4,25}) moved code by .05 or less.
- Early attention head groups found by attribution are destructive, not skill parts. L2 heads {9,10,19,30,31} dropped code by .20 but also wrecked facts and every translation skill and its control (some drops ~.9). L6 heads {11,22,25,26} did the same.
- The zh, ja and ru controls have tiny base scores, so they swing a lot. That blocks screening even for highly selective experts.

**Next steps:** define skills with stronger controls before re-screening L23 expert 21 for Russian and L22 experts {5,8,16} for Chinese.
